explanations.explanation: Seventy years is what Daniel understood from the sacred books. It was the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet, and it was about the desolation of Jerusalem (Daniel 9:2). Daniel read that number and it landed. I've been stuck in a dark place for a long stretch myself, so I know a number like that means something when you're counting.

Forty is a famous number in the Bible, but it isn't the one Daniel reads here. He understood from the sacred books that the desolation of Jerusalem would last seventy years. That's the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet. Forty is in the neighborhood, but seventy is the number on the page.

Four hundred years would be a LONG wait, friend. That's not what Daniel reads, though. He understood from the sacred books, according to the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet, that the desolation of Jerusalem would last seventy years. Four hundred is way past what the page says.

Daniel turns to the Lord God to seek Him "by prayer and petition, with fasting, sackcloth, and ashes." (Daniel 9:3) Sackcloth is rough cloth, the opposite of your comfiest sweater. I think a man dressed like that means business. He isn't treating this prayer as a quick stop on his way somewhere else.

explanations.answer: A feast with music and dancing
explanations.explanation: A feast with music and dancing is a party, and this prayer is no party. The text says Daniel came with fasting, sackcloth and ashes. Fasting is going without, so it's pretty much the opposite of a feast. Nobody's grabbing the good chair and asking where the music is.

Gold, silver and incense are fancy things, but Daniel doesn't bring any of them in this verse. He turns to the Lord God by prayer and petition, with fasting, sackcloth, and ashes. No gift basket, no shiny extras. It's just Daniel and his prayer.

Daniel doesn't stand off to the side pointing at everybody else. He says, "…we have sinned and done wrong. We have acted wickedly and rebelled." (Daniel 9:5) A few verses later he describes himself as "…confessing my sin and that of my people Israel…" (Daniel 9:20). That's a man putting himself right in the middle of it, so the answer is False.

False is right. Daniel says "we," and that "we" includes him: "…we have sinned and done wrong. We have acted wickedly and rebelled." (Daniel 9:5) Later he says he was "…confessing my sin and that of my people Israel…" (Daniel 9:20). No dodging, no "well, THEY did."

Prophets is it. Daniel says they did not listen to God's servants the prophets, who spoke in His name to their kings, leaders, fathers, and all the people of the land. Those messengers went from the top of the ladder all the way down. And Daniel says nobody listened.

Priests don't show up in this verse. Daniel says they didn't listen to God's servants the prophets, who spoke in His name to their kings, leaders, fathers, and all the people of the land. That's a lot of doors those prophets knocked on. The word that fits the blank is prophets.

Judges aren't named here. Daniel says the servants of God they didn't listen to were the prophets. They spoke in His name to the kings, the leaders, the fathers, and all the people of the land. The word for the blank is prophets.

Daniel says, "To the Lord our God belong compassion and forgiveness, even though we have rebelled against Him" (Daniel 9:9). Notice that he doesn't wait for the rebelling to stop before he says it. Shame covers the people, and compassion and forgiveness still belong to God. That's a good thing to know about Him.

Silence and distance is the opposite of what Daniel says. He says compassion and forgiveness belong to the Lord our God, even though they rebelled against Him (Daniel 9:9). Daniel is praying because he believes God is close enough to hear. Nobody prays this hard to a locked door.

Strength and secrecy don't show up in this verse. Daniel says compassion and forgiveness belong to the Lord our God, even though the people rebelled against Him (Daniel 9:9). Nothing in his prayer is hidden. He puts everything out in the open and names what God is like.

Moses is it. Daniel says the oath and the curse are "…written in the Law of Moses the servant of God…" (Daniel 9:11). He says it again in verse 13: "Just as it is written in the Law of Moses…" Daniel keeps pointing to what was written, and he doesn't argue with it.

Joshua, who led Israel after Moses (Joshua 1:1-2), isn't named in Daniel's prayer. Daniel says the oath and the curse were written in the Law of Moses the servant of God (Daniel 9:11). He comes back to it in verse 13, and he says Moses both times. So Moses fills the blank.

David, Israel's king (1 Samuel 16:13), isn't the name in this verse. Daniel says the oath and the curse were written in the Law of Moses the servant of God (Daniel 9:11). He says it again in verse 13. Moses is the one who fits the blank.

Daniel says the opposite. The disaster came, "…yet we have not sought the favor of the LORD our God by turning from our iniquities and giving attention to Your truth." (Daniel 9:13) The people didn't turn. That makes this statement False.

False is the one. Daniel says that after all this disaster, "…we have not sought the favor of the LORD our God by turning from our iniquities and giving attention to Your truth." (Daniel 9:13) He's telling it straight, with no spin. The people hadn't turned, and Daniel says so.

Egypt is right. Daniel says God "brought Your people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand," and made for Himself a name renowned to this day (Daniel 9:15). Daniel reaches back to something God already did. I think a man in a tight spot likes to remember that.

Assyria, a nation in the Bible, isn't the one in this verse. Daniel says God brought His people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand (Daniel 9:15). He says God made a name for Himself renowned to this day. Egypt is the word that fits the blank.

Moab, another nation named in the Bible, isn't in this verse. Daniel says God brought His people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand (Daniel 9:15). That's the act he brings up as he prays. Egypt fills the blank.

Daniel says it the other way around. He says, "…we are not presenting our petitions before You because of our righteous acts, but because of Your great compassion." (Daniel 9:18) He isn't walking up with a résumé. The answer is False.

False it is. Daniel says, "…we are not presenting our petitions before You because of our righteous acts, but because of Your great compassion." (Daniel 9:18) He isn't handing God a list of things they did right. He's leaning on God's compassion, and that's all.
True. Daniel prays, "For Your sake, O my God, do not delay…" (Daniel 9:19). It comes right after "O Lord, listen! O Lord, forgive! O Lord, hear and act!" He says it plainly and he means it.

Daniel actually does ask God not to delay. He prays, "For Your sake, O my God, do not delay…" (Daniel 9:19). It's the last thing he asks, right after "O Lord, listen! O Lord, forgive! O Lord, hear and act!" So the answer is True.

Gabriel is right. Daniel calls him "the man I had seen in the earlier vision," and says he came "in swift flight" (Daniel 9:21). Daniel is still praying when he shows up. I think that's some pretty fast service.

Michael, one of the chief princes (Daniel 10:13), isn't named in this verse. The text says Gabriel is the one who came to Daniel in swift flight. Daniel had seen him in the earlier vision (Daniel 9:21). Gabriel is the answer.

Elijah, the prophet who went up to heaven in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11), isn't the one who comes to Daniel here. The text says it's Gabriel, the man Daniel had seen in the earlier vision (Daniel 9:21). He arrives in swift flight. Gabriel is the answer.

Gabriel tells Daniel, "O Daniel, I have come now to give you insight and understanding." (Daniel 9:22) Daniel had already been reading and thinking about Jeremiah's word. Now Gabriel comes to give him more. Insight is the thing he brings, and he gets right to it.

A crown and a kingdom would be a lot to carry in swift flight. That's not what Gabriel says he brings. He says, "O Daniel, I have come now to give you insight and understanding." (Daniel 9:22) He's there to give Daniel understanding.

A sword and a shield aren't on Gabriel's delivery list. He says, "O Daniel, I have come now to give you insight and understanding." (Daniel 9:22) He doesn't hand over any gear. What he brings is understanding.

True. Gabriel says, "At the beginning of your petitions, an answer went out, and I have come to tell you…" (Daniel 9:23). The answer went out at the beginning, and Daniel was still praying when Gabriel arrived. The prayer had already been heard.

Gabriel says it did happen. He tells Daniel, "At the beginning of your petitions, an answer went out, and I have come to tell you…" (Daniel 9:23). The answer went out at the beginning of his petitions, and Gabriel arrived while Daniel was still praying. So the answer is True.

Put an end to sin is on the list. Gabriel says the seventy weeks are decreed "…to stop their transgression, to put an end to sin, to make atonement for iniquity…" (Daniel 9:24). It's right there in the middle of the list. These are big things, and they're meant for Daniel's people and holy city.

explanations.answer: Bring down the king of Persia
explanations.explanation: Gabriel doesn't say anything about bringing down the king of Persia. The seventy weeks are decreed for Daniel's people and holy city "…to stop their transgression, to put an end to sin, to make atonement for iniquity…" (Daniel 9:24). The list goes on from there. Putting an end to sin is the answer.

explanations.answer: Send the people back to Egypt
explanations.explanation: Going back to Egypt isn't anywhere on Gabriel's list. Earlier in his prayer, Daniel said God brought the people out of Egypt (Daniel 9:15). Gabriel says the seventy weeks are decreed "…to stop their transgression, to put an end to sin, to make atonement for iniquity…" (Daniel 9:24). Putting an end to sin is the answer.

True. Gabriel says the seventy weeks are decreed "…to bring in everlasting righteousness…" (Daniel 9:24). It sits in the same list as stopping transgression and making atonement. Everlasting is a big word, and Gabriel uses it.
Gabriel does say it. The seventy weeks are decreed "…to bring in everlasting righteousness…" (Daniel 9:24). It's part of the list he gives Daniel. So the answer is True.

Distress fits. Gabriel says Jerusalem "will be rebuilt with streets and a trench, but in times of distress." (Daniel 9:25) So the city gets rebuilt, and the time around it is hard. Both parts are in the same sentence.

Plenty isn't the word. Gabriel says Jerusalem will be rebuilt with streets and a trench, but in times of distress (Daniel 9:25). The little word "but" is a clue that the news turns. Distress fills the blank.

Celebration would be nice, but that's not what Gabriel says. He says Jerusalem will be rebuilt with streets and a trench, but in times of distress (Daniel 9:25). That "but" tells you the second half is heavier. Distress fills the blank.

Gabriel says nothing like that. He says, "…the end will come like a flood, and until the end there will be war; desolations have been decreed." (Daniel 9:26) Peace until the end isn't in that line, so the answer is False. It's a heavy verse, friend.
False is right. Gabriel says, "…until the end there will be war; desolations have been decreed." (Daniel 9:26) He doesn't promise peace until the end. It's a heavy line, and he says it straight.

Sacrifice and offering is right. Gabriel says, "…in the middle of the week he will put an end to sacrifice and offering." (Daniel 9:27) First he confirms a covenant with many for one week, and then comes the middle of that week. It's a serious part of the message.

The war and the flood come from the verse before. Gabriel says the end will come like a flood, and until the end there will be war (Daniel 9:26). In verse 27, the one who confirms a covenant puts an end to sacrifice and offering in the middle of the week. That's the answer.

The streets and the trench belong to the rebuilding of Jerusalem in verse 25. Verse 27 is about something else. In the middle of the week, the one who confirms the covenant will put an end to sacrifice and offering. That's the answer.
